extracted.intended_audience: literate general readers, poets, playwrights, and theatre-goers (early-18th-century audience of The Spectator)
extracted.subtask_description: A periodical-essay style set of prescriptive remarks on poetic technique (use of personification/allegory), qualities of social company and frolicking, standards for dress and appearance, and the theatrical role of audience instrumentation (the 'cat-call').

rubrics_metrics.name: Tender and moving representation of female characters (Eve)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Part of Eve in this Book is no less passionate, and apt to sway the Reader in her Favour. She is represented with great Tenderness as approaching Adam, but is spurn'd from him with a Spirit of Upbraiding and Indignation, conformable to the Nature of Man.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Passages wherein she renews her Addresses have something in them exquisitely moving and pathetick; Adam's reconcilement should be worked up in the same spirit of tenderness. Use such representation to engage reader's commiseration and to convey moral lessons (e.g., contrast between resolution to die and magnanimity of bearing miseries). Examples from the text (quoted lines) illustrate effective pathetic appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral clarity in character choices (bearing vs ending miseries)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Resolution of dying to end our Miseries, does not shew such a degree of Magnanimity as a Resolution to bear them, and submit to the Dispensations of Providence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a character contemplates extreme acts (e.g., seeking death to avoid guilt), represent opposing viewpoints (as Adam disapproves) to provide moral instruction. Present such thoughts delicately to highlight the moral without endorsing it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate use of imaginary persons/personification in epic poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: Such beautiful extended Allegories are certainly some of the finest Compositions of Genius: but, ... are not agreeable to the Nature of an Heroick Poem. When such Persons are introduced as principal Actors, and engaged in a Series of Adventures, they take too much upon them, and are by no means proper for an Heroick Poem, which ought to appear credible in its principal Parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short allegorical personifications (as in Homer and Virgil) are effective as poetical phrases to convey particular circumstances (e.g., 'the Hours brought him his Reward', 'Victory following Diomedes') and should be used sparingly. Avoid making personified abstractions (Sin, Death, Strength, Necessity) principal agents in sustained action for epic works, since that undermines credibility. Use scripture-style brief personification when grandeur is required; extensive fanciful description may be inferior to succinct scriptural mention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personification as brief poetical figure, not sustained dramatization
rubrics_metrics.description: These I have mentioned... are such short Allegories as are not designed to be taken in the literal Sense, but only to convey particular Circumstances to the Reader after an unusual and entertaining Manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer short, expressive uses of personification that function as poetic shorthand for feelings or circumstances; treat them as figures of speech rather than characters with series of actions. Examples: Flight and Fear as inseparable companions; the Hours unbarring the Gates of Light.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualities of a pleasant companion / proper frolicking
rubrics_metrics.description: Irregularity in its self is not what creates Pleasure and Mirth; but to see a Man who knows what Rule and Decency are, descend from them agreeably in our Company, is what denominates him a pleasant Companion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: True frolick is 'the Play of the Mind' consisting of various and unforced sallies of imagination. A pleasant companion: (a) observes rule and decency and can descend agreeably from them, (b) contributes and receives to the company's pleasure without overrating his own part, (c) avoids loud, mischievous, airy dullness and actions that shock others, (d) uses mimicry that does not debase the person represented. Examples/antipatterns: vulgar practical jokes that cause harm or public scandal are not true frolick; pantomime-like, tasteful mimicry enhances company.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confine frolic/behavior to appropriate place (analogy to unity of time/place)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Writers of Plays have what they call Unity of Time and Place to give a Justness to their Representation; and it would not be amiss if all who pretend to be Companions, would confine their Action to the Place of Meeting: For a Frolick carried farther may be better performed by other Animals than Men.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep jovial or disorderly behaviours within the bounds of the social setting that receives them. Excessive frolicking that spills into public or inappropriate spaces is uncivil and unbecoming; restraint preserves agreeableness and prevents mischief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appearances and dress as legitimate social strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: It is a Justice due to the Character of one who suffers hard Reflections... that appearing to be otherwise is not only pardonable but necessary... I shall engage myself no further than in the modest Defence of two plain Suits a Year: ... a Stranger of tolerable Sense dressd like a Gentleman, will be better received by those of Quality above him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modest concealment of narrow circumstances by reasonable dress is excusable and can be necessary to gain acquaintance with higher circles; but avoid foppery and exceeding one's means. Practical rules: maintain modest but genteel appearance (e.g., two plain suits a year), use conversation and reserved behavior to signal learning, and avoid ostentatious expenses that compromise probity. Appearance influences first impressions more than displayed learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of the cat-call as theatrical criticism / instrument of audience feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: The Cat-call... very much Improves the Sound of Nonsense, and often goes along with the Voice of the Actor... It has often supplied the Place of the antient Chorus... The Cat-call has struck a Damp into Generals, and frighted Heroes off the Stage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the cat-call as a theatrical device for audience critique: it can signal contempt for bad verse or performance, mark violations of dramatic unities (one 'squeak' to denote violation), distinguish whether the player or poet is the target, and use different 'notes' (smut-note, fustian-note, stupid-note) to express particular criticisms. Use appropriately and contextually; it is dramatick and stage-appropriate but improper in private serenades.
